texts: Reading a size chart on USFans: body size, garment width and ease

A medium hoodie can have a chest marked 96 cm in one chart and 56 cm in another. Those figures may both be correct. Before purchasing through USFans, establish what each supplier measured, whose body or garment they measured, and how a familiar piece of clothing compares.
Work out what the chart describes

Start at the top of the chart, including any diagram above it. A seller may give recommended body measurements, measurements of the finished garment, or a weight-and-height suggestion. Reading one number without that context can send you to a different size. A recommended chest circumference describes the wearer. A finished chest circumference describes the garment. The latter usually includes space between fabric and body; the amount varies with cut, stretch and intended fit. Two shirts intended for the same wearer can therefore have very different finished measurements.

A diagram adds information that a translated column heading can lose. An arrow running horizontally across the front of a garment suggests a flat width. A loop around a model's torso suggests circumference. An arrow from shoulder to hem might indicate length, but its starting point matters. If the chart only shows a size letter and a number, keep the ambiguity visible in your notes. The product picture can suggest how a garment is supposed to look; it cannot tell you which interpretation the seller used for the chart. Ask for the method before committing to a marginal size.
Build a comparison around a garment you wear

Pick a piece that fits the way you want this purchase to fit. For a winter overshirt, use one that goes comfortably over the layer you expect to wear underneath it. Comparing against a fitted T-shirt would answer a different question. Close buttons or zips, lay the garment on a flat surface and let it settle. Straighten obvious folds without pulling the fabric taut. Measure between the underarm seams across the front and record the distance, units and orientation. A photograph of your tape placement can be more valuable than a list of numbers alone.

Measure any feature that would change your decision. A tall buyer may be able to tolerate an extra centimetre of width but need a very particular sleeve or body length. A cropped jacket may fit across the chest while exposing a shirt beneath it. Write down an acceptable interval based on garments you actually own, if you can. Someone happy with shirts measuring 52 to 55 cm flat has a more useful reference than someone who writes only “normally medium.” This interval describes your preference; it is not a manufacturing tolerance or a promise from the seller.
Match the measurement method before calculating

Suppose your reference hoodie measures 56 cm flat across the chest. A chart listing a 112 cm finished chest circumference is consistent with that width for a simple, reasonably symmetrical garment laid flat. Dividing the circumference by two gives a 56 cm comparison point. If 112 cm instead describes the recommended wearer's chest, dividing by two does not tell you how wide the hoodie will be. Likewise, an entry of 56 cm described as a half chest can be compared directly to your flat measurement. These are examples to illustrate units, not a size recommendation.

Length requires a different check. A back measured from the seam at the base of the collar to the middle hem often has a different result from a line beginning at the highest point near the shoulder. Repeat the seller's stated method on your reference garment before comparing. A dropped shoulder complicates sleeve measurements: the sleeve seam begins lower on the arm, so the sleeve alone can measure shorter while the cuff still reaches the same point. If the chart measures from the centre back of the neck instead, include that distance on your reference piece too.
Distinguish the selected option from the product family

A single listing can put standard, oversized and cropped versions next to each other. Check whether the chart changes when you select the version you want. Inspect the wording above the diagram and look for model numbers shared with the option buttons. An excellent chart for the standard version can produce a poor decision on the cropped version. Save the selected option wording in its original form, a short description in your own words and the chart that applies to it. Keep the product link beside those records so you can revisit the same offer.

If two versions share one chart and the photographs suggest different proportions, state the conflict precisely. Ask which version has the listed length and whether the dimension includes the collar. A question framed as “will medium fit me?” leaves the seller or agent guessing at your preferred fit. A question framed as “does the short black medium measure 63 cm from the back collar seam to the centre hem?” identifies the version, size, endpoints and number that drive your decision. Keep that conversation attached to the purchase reference in your records.
Use the warehouse photograph to test the remaining uncertainty

The USFans beginner's guide describes warehouse inspection and the photographs available after receipt. Check the photographs attached to your specific warehouse entry. A clear label can establish what size is printed on that piece. It cannot establish how wide it is when laid flat. If a few centimetres will affect whether you keep it, ask through the order channel whether the measurement you need can be obtained, what it would cost if it is an additional service, and whether there is enough time to review it before the next decision.

For a useful photograph, request the garment flat with both endpoints visible. Tell the person handling it exactly where to place the tape. Look for the zero mark, correct units and alignment with the seams. If the start disappears beneath a fold, explain which view is missing. A close-up of the final reading might make the number easy to read while making the position impossible to check. Review shape as well as size: a curved hem, wide shoulder and elasticated waistband can change how two garments with the same recorded chest measurement sit on the body.
Make the size decision legible a week later

Keep a compact record with the seller listing, selected version, size, seller measurement method and reference measurement. Add the warehouse observation on a new line so that it stays distinct from the seller's claim. For example, write “chart gives 110 cm finished chest, my preferred hoodie is 54–56 cm flat, actual item photographed at 55 cm across underarms.” With that information the reason for keeping the size remains clear even after other packages arrive. If the methods do not match, record the question instead of manufacturing a precise comparison.

When a piece falls close to the edge of your acceptable range, consider the practical consequence. A slightly roomy overshirt may still layer comfortably. A closely fitted non-stretch shirt with the same difference might be difficult to fasten. A shorter length may be part of the cut you wanted. Use the measured feature together with the intended use, then check the available options on your current USFans order if you need a clarification or change. This makes the final choice traceable to the garment you want and the evidence for the particular unit you are buying.

For knitwear, note whether the garment was relaxed when measured. Two flat widths taken with different tension are difficult to compare, even when the tape placement matches. If the garment will be layered, try your reference piece over that layer before recording the acceptable range. This catches a surprisingly common oversight: measuring a sweatshirt that is comfortable over a T-shirt and using that result to choose a coat intended to fit over the sweatshirt itself.
When USFans cannot read a seller link: prepare a manual purchase request

An empty product page leaves two questions open. The marketplace listing might still exist, and the agent might still be able to purchase the exact option. Establish each fact separately before paying or accepting a similar product.
Identify what actually failed

Begin by returning to the page where the link came from. A spreadsheet row might point to an agent, a seller listing, a shop collection, or an image album. These destinations contain different information. A purchase request needs an identifiable item and a seller who can supply it. An album may show a jacket from six angles while providing neither a price nor an orderable option. Follow the seller link supplied with the entry when there is one. Record which page opens successfully and which page fails. “The marketplace page opens but the agent page shows no options” is a useful diagnosis.

If a link came from a messaging app, check whether the pasted text includes a sentence, a product title or punctuation alongside the address. Retain the original message, then copy just the link intended for the item. Open it normally and compare the displayed seller and item with the saved find. A redirect to a shop homepage means you still need the individual product page. A removed listing is a separate problem: an agent cannot derive current stock merely from an old picture. Capture the page state and date so the person helping you can distinguish an import problem from an unavailable offer.
Recover enough information to identify the exact offer

Write down the source marketplace, seller name, product title and item identifier where visible. Use the same marketplace when comparing identifiers. A number from a warehouse record refers to a different system from a number in a Weidian product URL. A copied product name alone is weak evidence because sellers can reuse it across different pieces. Look for a model reference, a distinguishing construction detail, and original option wording. In a full product family, the item number can remain the same for both the standard coat and a shorter version.

Photographs can help locate the seller, but keep discovery and confirmation separate. USFans describes product-link, keyword and photo searches in its beginner's guide. Use a name search when the original title contains distinctive words, and a picture search when the available image clearly shows the model. If several shops reuse the same catalogue image, keep more than one candidate until you can inspect their option lists. A candidate without the requested size or model is not an equivalent purchase, even if an image-search result puts it first. Note any difference that would change the amount you pay or the garment you receive.
Turn a manual request into an unambiguous specification

Once the original item is identified, make a short order note. Include the seller URL, the original text of the required option, size, colour, quantity and any indispensable feature. Avoid relying on position in a menu: the third blue swatch on a desktop screen may not occupy the same position after a listing changes or on a smaller display. If option labels are ambiguous, attach the selected-state screenshot and explain what the label means in context. Name the component you want when a listing sells individual pieces and sets from the same page.

An illustrative order note might read: “Please check availability of two navy overshirts, model B with the straight hem, both size L. The seller calls the option Navy B. I need the shirts only. Please ask before changing model, colour or size.” That note answers a question about quantity and places a clear limit on substitution. If you would accept an alternative, state the exact alternative and any condition, such as a maximum unit price. A later conversation about an unavailable option is much shorter when it begins with a written record of what the buyer already approved.
Confirm the amount and the route before submitting payment

Ask through the current USFans order channel whether the listing and option can be purchased in this situation. Use the options actually displayed in the account. A manual or assisted purchase is an inquiry until the agent has identified what can be ordered and at what price. Changing marketplace stock, seller restrictions or a minimum order can affect the outcome. Check the unit, number of units and currency on the confirmation. If the item is sold by the pair, for example, a quantity of two could mean two pairs. Quote the unit back before approving a substantial order.

Budget product price and domestic delivery together for the purchasing stage, while recording them separately. Keep later international freight as a different cost. Consider an example where an advertised item costs 70 yuan and the seller quotes 8 yuan domestic delivery for the order. Two units would give a product subtotal of 140 yuan; a single shared delivery charge would make 148 yuan before any separately listed amounts. If the 8 yuan applies per unit instead, the arithmetic changes. The example gives a checking method, not a USFans rate. Read the actual confirmation rather than copying the catalogue's lowest displayed price.
Handle partial answers and changed specifications

Sometimes the response resolves one question and leaves another open. “Available” might refer to the model but not the size, or “same price” might refer to the product before domestic delivery. Reply with the unresolved question and quote the relevant line from your order note. Avoid sending a fresh set of pictures without identifying which one is the selected version. If the seller proposes a substitute, ask for its own listing, distinguishing features, price and size information. Save the proposal as a new option so it does not overwrite the details of the original request.

Use the purchase decision to control risk. When the image, option text and unit agree, you can decide whether the offer meets your needs. When the seller can only promise “something similar,” decide whether the uncertainty is acceptable for this specific purchase. For an item personalized with a name, an ambiguous order note can lead to a difficult disagreement. For a standard item you may simply prefer to wait for an identifiable listing. Check applicable cancellation and after-sales terms on the current order before authorizing work that changes the product. Record a decision to decline as clearly as a decision to proceed.
Use the order record once the item arrives

After purchase, link the seller reference to the USFans order number and any later warehouse reference. Keep those as separate fields. When warehouse photos become available, return to the manual specification and check the few details that distinguished this purchase in the first place. For the overshirt example, look for two units, the straight hem, the correct option label and the requested size. A photo of a folded navy shirt can be consistent with several different models. Ask for the missing view if one of your original conditions cannot be verified from the supplied pictures.

If the order eventually succeeds, save the corrected seller link and date alongside the original failed link. The next person reviewing your record can then tell which address imported correctly, which details required a manual conversation and what the warehouse actually received. If the seller withdraws the listing instead, retain the final response and close the inquiry without treating it as an order. That distinction matters when reconciling payments or counting pieces for an outbound parcel. A manual purchase works best when the final record is as precise as a normal product checkout, even though the information came from several separate screens.
Ordering several 1688 variants through USFans: units, minimums and price tiers

A wholesale listing can look affordable until the buyer discovers that the displayed unit is a pack, that the minimum applies to each colour, or that the price shown belongs to a quantity they do not intend to buy. Resolve those details together before submitting a USFans order.
Find the unit behind the price

Start with the live marketplace offer. Note the seller, listing identifier and date, then read the unit printed next to the price or quantity selector. A page selling socks may use a pair, a pack of pairs or a full assortment as the orderable unit. Attractive photographs of six colours do not establish whether the buyer receives six pairs. Check the text attached to the selected option, the package contents and the order summary. If these disagree, ask which rule applies to the specific option. Keep the response with the order rather than relying on a remembered interpretation of the listing.

Write the desired purchase in ordinary language before touching the selector. For example, “I need three individual navy pairs and three grey pairs, all the same size.” Translate that into the seller's units only after the unit is known. If the unit is a pack of three identical pairs, the request could be two units. If it is an assorted pack containing several fixed colours, two units may produce a completely different mix. An item title saying “six colours available” describes a choice and says nothing about the contents of one pack. This check takes less time than untangling an unwanted assortment at the warehouse.
Separate the seller's minimum from its quantity discounts

A minimum order tells you whether the seller will accept a purchase at all. A price tier tells you the unit rate applicable at a particular quantity. They can appear close together on the screen, but they answer different questions. A seller might accept two units at one price and offer a lower rate starting at ten. Selecting two would satisfy the minimum while leaving the cheaper tier out of reach. On a listing offering multiple sizes, check whether the minimum applies to the entire item, each option, a specific combination or a full style run.

Suppose a sample offer lists 2–9 units at 24 yuan and 10 or more at 20 yuan. Six units at the first rate cost 144 yuan. Ten at the second rate cost 200 yuan. The second rate is lower per unit, yet it requires a larger total payment and leaves four additional units to ship or store. These are illustrative figures. When deciding what to buy, compare total product cost at your intended quantity, then include any separately quoted domestic delivery. Treat the lower unit rate as valuable only if the extra pieces serve a purpose and the seller confirms the mix qualifies.
Test what “mixed colours” actually permits

A mixed order can mean different things to different sellers. One seller may combine colours within one model and size. Another may allow different sizes of a single colour. A third may sell a preset assortment without allowing the buyer to choose the mix. Write down the distribution you want as separate lines and ask whether those lines can count toward the same minimum. If the listing already describes the rule, save the relevant wording. Use the original option codes beside your translated descriptions, especially where adjacent colours have nearly identical names.

Take a second example. You need four blue medium pieces, two blue large pieces and four green medium pieces. That makes ten units in total. If a ten-unit tier applies across the listing, your mix may qualify. If ten units are required per colour, neither the six blue nor the four green qualify independently. If the seller counts each size-colour combination separately, there are three groups. The arithmetic is simple once the grouping rule is known. Until then, the total on a spreadsheet row is only a planning figure. Ask for confirmation of both the mix and the price before treating the order as approved.
Carry the agreed quantities into the USFans order

USFans describes selecting product options and quantities after loading a marketplace link. Check the imported selections against the 1688 offer you just examined. If a tier table or package description did not import clearly, keep the seller page and ask about the unresolved detail through the order channel. Enter a separate selection for each combination when the interface permits it. In the remarks, describe how many physical pieces you expect from each line. This makes a pack-based purchase intelligible to someone who sees only the order units later.

Keep a simple reconciliation record with four columns: seller option, order units, pieces per unit and expected physical pieces. Three packs of two make six pieces; three single pieces make three. Include the size on each line even when a single size appears throughout the order. A later stock message may propose a substitution on only one colour. Check whether the change also affects the total price tier or minimum. An offer meeting the threshold before one unavailable line is removed might no longer do so afterwards. Request the revised subtotal and any change to domestic delivery in the same conversation.
Inspect the delivery at the right level

USFans notes that products purchased from 1688 can follow different inspection standards. Read the inspection terms that apply to the actual order. Before buying, decide what evidence you need for the quantity and option mix. A single outer carton marked with a model number can help identify the shipment without proving how many pieces are inside or how the colours are distributed. If opening a sealed retail pack matters to a future return, check the conditions before requesting it. A photo request should specify whether you need a count of packages, loose units, labels or all three.

Suppose the warehouse photographs four sealed bags containing three pairs each. If your order was for twelve pairs in four identical packs, this can support an outer-pack count. If it was for six navy and six grey pairs, a photograph showing only the outer carton leaves the colour split unresolved. Ask for readable package labels first. If labels distinguish colours but not sizes, name the remaining question rather than asking for the whole inspection to be repeated. Keep any seller packing list in context: it records the seller's stated contents and can guide inspection, while pictures of the received items provide separate evidence.
Resolve short deliveries before treating the order as complete

If ten units were ordered and eight appear in the first warehouse entry, look for a second domestic shipment before assuming a shortage. Compare seller tracking numbers with the agent order and warehouse entries. Then send a concise account of the expected and observed quantities. Identify which combinations are missing. “Two units short” is less actionable than “both green large units are absent; six blue and two green medium units are present.” Ask whether a second package is pending, whether another option was supplied, or whether the seller needs to address a short shipment.

Finalize the order record only when the seller mix, amounts paid and warehouse count agree or when the remaining difference has a documented resolution. If a partial refund is offered, record the units it covers and the currency and destination of the refund. If the seller resends missing pieces, wait for their own tracking reference and inspect the replacement mix. Finally, select only the warehouse entries you actually intend to forward. This closes the loop between the wholesale quantity shown on the listing and the physical pieces that will occupy your international parcel.
Finding a missing USFans product link from a photo

An image search can recover a useful lead when all you have is a saved photograph. Turning that lead into an identifiable seller listing takes a second kind of work. The result must match the features that matter, open to an available option, and carry enough information for you to tell another buyer exactly what you found.
Decide which object you are looking for

A saved outfit photograph can contain shoes, trousers, a jacket and a bag. Start by naming the object and the detail that made you save the picture. Perhaps it was the shape of a side pocket on the jacket or the way a strap attaches to the bag. Create a crop that isolates the object while preserving its outline. Leave the relevant feature in the frame. A tight crop around a graphic can make the search engine return another garment carrying the same graphic, and a full outfit image can make the trousers dominate a search intended for the jacket.

Keep an untouched copy of the source picture. Use copies to experiment with a wider crop and a close detail. If the item appears in several views, save them together instead of assuming the most attractive view will be the most informative. A front view might be enough to find a product family, while the back view separates two versions. Remove visible usernames, addresses or parcel labels from anything you upload. For this task the useful evidence is the product itself. A buyer's shipping label adds no value to a visual search and exposes information unrelated to identifying the item.
Use two different search routes with a purpose

The USFans beginner's guide describes finding products by marketplace link, keyword and uploaded image. If the original URL is missing, begin with the image route. Save a small set of promising results and note why each looks relevant. Run a keyword search after you have gathered labels, model names or original seller terminology from those results. That second search can locate an offer whose main photograph looks different but whose construction is a closer match. Multiple search routes answer the same question with different evidence.

On an independent USFans spreadsheet, image results are limited by what its catalogue contains and how its search matches images. The first result is a candidate rather than proof of origin. If nothing looks close, use a second crop or another angle. When every result shows the same large print on completely different garments, switch from a print crop to a whole-item image. When the silhouettes match but the wrong pocket or sole keeps appearing, bring that detail into a tighter crop. Change one aspect of the query at a time so you can see which change led to a better candidate.
Compare stable features before reading the price

Open each candidate and compare the features the original image actually shows. With a jacket, check the number and angle of external pockets, hood attachment, cuff adjustment and seam placement. With a bag, inspect the strap attachment, hardware layout and how the opening closes. Compare left and right in relation to the item rather than the screen; a mirrored social photo can reverse the image. Colour is a weak first filter when lighting or editing differs. A pocket in a completely different position is usually more informative for identification than a small change in shade.

Keep a simple shortlist. A line such as “same pocket geometry, wrong ribbed cuff” is more helpful than a star rating without a reason. If all distinguishing details are hidden, leave the candidate unresolved. Seek another view instead of adding confidence because the overall styling looks familiar. A seller photograph reused by several shops establishes that the image circulates, not that each shop supplies the same item. Distinguish a listing that uses the exact photograph from a listing that offers visible evidence of the construction you actually want.
Compare listings and options separately

Once a candidate looks plausible, open the linked marketplace offer and record the marketplace, seller and item identifier. Different agent URLs can lead to the same seller item, while two marketplace listings can use indistinguishable promotional images. Inspect the option menu on the live offer. Does it include the colour and version you want? Does selecting the option change the picture or product description? If the product family has multiple versions, save the exact selected wording. A link that opens the right family on a default variant can still produce an incorrect purchase.

Suppose your picture shows a tote with a zip and a removable strap. One candidate has the same body shape and a magnetic fastening, while another offers a zip but only on a larger version. The first fails the fastening requirement. The second might identify the product family while leaving your intended size uncertain. If size and fastening are both important, request confirmation of that combination before proceeding. If you only sought a similar shape, you may be happy with either. The record should state which question was answered: original source, same apparent model, or a suitable alternative.
Use historical QC photographs selectively

An available warehouse photograph from another order can show how a unit from a listing looked outside the seller's studio. Check whether the marketplace item and selected option are identifiable. A picture of a navy medium garment can show a seam detail shared by a family, but it cannot tell you the dimensions of an unpictured large. Look for specific evidence you could point to in a dispute: a visible zip, an option label, a pair count, or a readable measurement. Save the reference separately from the pictures of your own future order.

Technical limitations matter. A bag photographed from one side can hide a second compartment. Shoes seen from above reveal little about outsole construction. A neutral backdrop under strong lighting can make two different colours appear close. Instead of concluding that the search is wrong, identify the missing angle and decide whether obtaining it would change the outcome. If the model identification matters enough, ask the seller or agent a short, checkable question. A request like “please confirm whether the small black version has both the internal zip and the removable strap in this photo” gives the recipient something concrete to verify.
Save a result that will survive a changed listing

When you decide on a candidate, save both the original marketplace link and the USFans link, the seller name, exact option text and date. Add a brief sentence describing the evidence that carried the decision. A spreadsheet entry saying “found it” becomes difficult to interpret once a seller changes the hero image or translates the options differently. A note saying “same pocket shape and cuffs; option B shown with detachable hood; checked seller listing” gives the next review a starting point. Mark what remains uncertain instead of letting it disappear from the shortlist.

Before purchase, reopen the saved source and reselect the intended option. Check stock, price, quantity and any special requirement on the live order. If a listing disappears between research and payment, return to the saved candidates and repeat only the unresolved identification steps. After warehouse intake, inspect the entry tied to your own order reference. This closes the distance between a photograph you liked and a product you can evaluate. Even when the original seller remains unknown, a transparent record lets you decide whether the available alternative meets your needs without pretending that an image match proved more than it did.
A USFans order note for a personalised print: from spelling to placement

A custom shirt can arrive with the right name in the wrong position, the correct number in the wrong typeface, or a perfectly legible print on the wrong garment. Separate the information the seller must reproduce from the features the buyer simply expects, and agree on how each will be checked.
Establish what can actually be personalised

Start at the seller's selected option, rather than the photograph of a finished example. A listing might sell a blank garment, a printed version and the printing service as separate choices. Read the current option description and ask which choice includes the work. Confirm whether the shop accepts the requested characters, accents, punctuation, colours and number of lines. A seller may offer only a fixed alphabet or a preset typeface. An invitation to leave a note does not by itself establish that every element of the design is configurable.

Keep the USFans product link beside the seller listing and chosen option. USFans describes using order remarks for requirements and Order Enquiry for details during purchasing. Those are useful channels for recording a request; a remark alone does not show that the seller accepted it. Ask which details require seller confirmation before production begins. If a change would make the piece unusable, say so explicitly. For example, a club shirt ordered for a group may need the same lettering on every piece, while a single gift may require an accent unavailable in the default character set.
Prepare a copy-ready specification

Give each custom element a separate line. Identify the base garment, model code, size and colour first. Then provide the exact text as it should appear, including spaces and capitalisation. Label the player's name, back number and sleeve marks separately if the design includes them. Do not rely on quotation marks alone to indicate where text begins and ends; punctuation intended only as a delimiter can be interpreted as literal print. A heading such as “Back name, exactly seven letters” makes the following line easier to read.

Check the specification from the garment owner's perspective. Imagine a hypothetical print reading MARTÍN and 07. The accent is part of the name and the leading zero is part of the number. A seller might normalize the name to MARTIN or treat 07 as the number seven when entering it into another system. Ask the recipient to repeat the intended text in writing or supply a proof if that service is available. Keep any agreed substitute spelling in a separate message. Silence about an unsupported accent is different from the buyer explicitly accepting a version without it.
Define placement from the garment itself

Describe left and right as worn. “Left chest as worn” identifies the wearer's left side even when the photographer faces the garment and sees it on the right of the screen. If the text belongs on a sleeve, specify which sleeve, which direction it should read and whether the reference image has been mirrored. For centred back lettering, identify the centre line and whether the text should sit straight, follow an arc, or align with a panel or stripe. An image with a marked rectangle can help communicate placement when written instructions alone leave two plausible interpretations.

Only request numerical precision the seller can genuinely offer. A placement instruction measured from a collar seam is clearer than “a little lower,” yet production may still have an agreed tolerance. Ask how the shop measures and which variation it can accept before ordering. On different garment sizes, a fixed width can look relatively larger or smaller. For a group purchase, ask whether design dimensions scale with the garment or stay fixed. Save the actual answer. A mock-up created for a medium shirt might not predict how the same lettering fills the back panel of a much smaller shirt.
Keep a proof tied to the correct unit

Distinguish a sample image, a digital mock-up for your request and an image of the finished piece. A sample can show available fonts or materials. A digital proof can confirm spelling and layout if the seller supplies one. Only a picture of the completed garment can establish which design ended up on that physical unit. Label the files accordingly. If the seller sends a revised proof, keep its revision date or number. Approve that specific revision in writing and say which earlier instruction it supersedes.

For several garments, use a row per item. Place each row's buyer reference, base garment, size, colour, name and number together. Read across the row to check that each set of details belongs to the same piece, then read down the name and number columns to catch accidental duplicates or shifted lines. A common mistake is producing every requested name and every requested number, but pairing two names with the opposite numbers. Recording the complete combination per unit prevents that error from disappearing inside a list of individually correct totals.
Clarify cost and the last point for changes

Ask for the amount attributable to the base item and the amount attributable to custom work. Check whether a price covers one printed area, several lines, both sides or each individual garment. If the seller sends a separate payment link for printing, establish exactly which base order it belongs to. Keep one written record of the agreed quantity, option and total in the original currency. If more than one party has to approve a proof, avoid submitting contradictory responses from separate conversations.

Before authorizing work, check the current seller and agent conditions for changes, cancellations and returns on personalised items. The timing matters: correcting a note while the seller is checking availability can be different from asking for a change after printing. Do not assume that a normal return arrangement applies to custom work, or that every error has the same remedy. If the seller cannot confirm an essential detail before starting, consider waiting. A clearly documented decision to proceed without a proof is still a decision about uncertainty, and it should be made by the person who will use the garment.
Inspect the finished piece in a reproducible order

At warehouse intake, check the base garment first. Read the size label, option and identifying features, then compare the full design with the approved proof. Read the text character by character, including punctuation and accents. Check leading zeros, line order and which side of the garment carries the print. Use an overall view for alignment and a closer view for small letters. If the entire photograph seems reversed, look at another readable object in the frame or request a different view before treating the print itself as reversed.

If a difference remains, send the order reference, the approved proof and the photograph of the actual piece together. Describe the precise discrepancy, such as “the proof shows 07 and the finished back shows 7.” Ask which options are available under the order conditions. Preserve the packaging and tags until the response clarifies what the seller needs. For a group order, identify only the affected units and continue tracking the rest separately. This yields a clear record of what was requested, what was accepted and what actually arrived, which is much more useful than a general complaint that the design looks wrong.

Before closing the record, check the spelling one final time against its intended source, such as the spelling supplied by the person receiving the garment. A perfect match between the seller proof and the finished piece can still reproduce a mistake in the buyer's first message. Saving that original instruction makes the source of a discrepancy clear and helps avoid placing a repeat order with the same error.
Does a USFans listing include the whole outfit? Reading set and single-piece options

A photograph can show a jacket, trousers and a belt even when the option currently selected buys just the belt. Read the offer as a list of included pieces, then check the quantity arriving at the warehouse against that original list.
Describe the purchase before interpreting the image

Start by deciding which pieces you intend to buy. A matching outfit can involve a complete set sold under one option, individually priced separates, or a choice between those arrangements. If your goal is a coordinated jacket and trouser combination, write down the style, colour and size you need for each. Someone who wears different jacket and trouser sizes may find a fixed-size set unsuitable even when the individual pieces look perfect. Knowing that requirement in advance helps you identify the question worth asking before purchase.

Review the seller's live offer and keep its link beside the USFans page. Inspect the text attached to the chosen option, the option image, unit price and quantity. The main photograph may stay the same while the purchase changes from trousers only to a two-piece combination. Change one selector at a time and observe what changes in the summary. If the price drops sharply when you select an accessory, check the name of the unit before assuming the whole outfit has been discounted. Record enough detail to reopen the offer and reproduce the same selection later.
Identify which combinations the seller allows

Look for a menu that describes the contents separately from colour and size. A label translated as “suit” might refer to a full set, a suit-style jacket or a product family. Inspect any original seller text, model code or explanatory chart that ties a particular option to the included items. If the description and the selected picture disagree, ask for a count and name of the pieces. “Does option B include one top and one pair of trousers?” leaves less room for misunderstanding than “does it come like the photo?”

Suppose the seller offers top only in small through large, trousers only in the same three sizes, and complete sets in medium or large. For a small top and medium trousers, a buyer might need two separate selections rather than one complete set. Compare the actual cost, quantity, availability and seller's willingness to supply the intended combination. If two colours carry similar translations, make sure the shades are intended to coordinate. Two pieces from unrelated listings marketed under the same English colour name can be made of different fabrics or dyed to different shades.
Compare the actual cost of a set with the cost of separates

Choose the exact variants first, then calculate the cost of obtaining the intended outfit. In an illustrative offer, a jacket at 85 yuan and trousers at 60 yuan make a product subtotal of 145 yuan, while a complete set is offered at 135 yuan. The set costs less only if it contains both pieces in suitable sizes. Include any domestic shipping charge according to the seller's actual checkout. One delivery charge shared by two selections behaves differently from delivery quoted per separately purchased piece. Keep the source currency visible when comparing.

A third piece pictured alongside the set can change the calculation. If a matching belt is important, check whether either offer actually includes it. If the belt costs a further 12 yuan and is excluded from both offers, add it to both totals. If just one offer includes it, note that the offers now have different contents. Do the same for removable straps, hoods or liners when they are essential. Avoid turning a set comparison into a comparison of two unrelated totals simply because the thumbnail photographs happen to look alike.
Write an order note that survives fulfilment

For a fixed set, record the set option, selected colour, size and number of sets, followed by the expected pieces in each. For separates, use one line per variant and link them with a short reference such as “outfit A.” Include relevant size codes exactly as displayed by the seller. USFans's beginner guide describes selecting options and quantities and using remarks for purchasing requirements. A concise note provides context if the agent or seller has to ask about stock, mismatched sizes or a proposed substitution.

Define which substitutions require your decision. If the jacket is out of stock, would you still want the trousers? If the set in navy is unavailable, would black be acceptable for both pieces or only one? Write “please ask before purchasing only part of the outfit” when a partial order would defeat your purpose. Check the seller's actual options if a component becomes unavailable. A complete set price may no longer apply if the seller can supply just one piece. Save the revised description and total before agreeing to a different purchase.
Check warehouse intake one component at a time

When a warehouse entry appears, identify which order and domestic shipment it belongs to. A top and trousers purchased separately may arrive in different bags or shipments. A complete set may be packed together and show as one warehouse entry. Neither pattern alone proves a shortage. Compare the expected contents with the entry and its photographs. Look for a view showing the pieces together and separate label views if the sizes matter. If a tiny accessory is missing from the overview, ask whether it is inside a pocket or separate protective sleeve before reporting it as absent.

Use a component list for matching sets with complex construction. For a three-piece weatherproof outfit it might read outer jacket, removable liner and trousers. An assembled jacket can hide the liner attachment in a folded photo. Request the view that will answer the question, such as the inner fasteners or the pieces laid out separately. Look at colour consistency in the same frame under the same light when possible. A dark jacket photographed in daylight and dark trousers photographed under warmer warehouse lighting may look different even if the cloth matches.
Resolve differences without losing track of the rest

If a component appears wrong, tell USFans which paid option you selected, what it included and which piece differs. Attach the seller description and a warehouse picture that identifies the affected unit. Ask what the seller requires if a return or exchange is possible. A seller could require the full set, including packaging, even when only one piece has an issue. Check the current terms and preserve everything while the answer is pending. Avoid authorizing packaging removal or dispatching one piece internationally if it might be needed for the same case.

Finally, record the actual number of physical pieces you are sending and which warehouse entries contain them. If an exchange replaces only the trousers, inspect the replacement colour and size against the jacket you retained. If the seller refunds an absent belt, mark the belt as resolved by refund rather than received. When you eventually open the outbound parcel, the record should show the intended outfit, any agreed changes and the pieces that actually travelled. That makes a set intelligible from the original photograph through purchase, inspection and international delivery.

A useful final test is whether someone opening the parcel without the original model picture could tell what belongs together. A description such as “grey set B, one short jacket and one straight trouser, detachable belt inside the jacket pocket” passes that test. A description such as “grey outfit from the first photo” leaves almost every important feature implicit. This also helps with repeat purchases when only one worn component needs replacing and the seller still lists the separates.
Requesting a shoe insole measurement on USFans

An EU size printed on a shoe and a length photographed on a ruler answer different questions. To use either one well, match the shoe, measurement method and intended fit before comparing numbers. A cropped picture of a number beside a shoe rarely resolves all three.
Decide which length you actually need

Foot length describes a person. Removable insole length describes an insert. Internal shoe length concerns the space inside a shoe and can be difficult to measure accurately. Outsole length includes material outside that space. A seller's chart might use any of these, or might only show conversions between size systems. Read the chart heading and diagram before interpreting a centimetre value. When the chart simply says “length,” look for the endpoints in the diagram or ask what was measured. Converting a number to another unit does nothing to fix a mismatch between two different measurements.

State the intended use in your own notes. A close-fitting court shoe, a cushioned walking shoe and a boot worn with thick socks can feel different even when two removable insoles measure the same length. Width, toe-box shape, volume and the heel construction can matter as much as length. Pick the unresolved question. If you already know the model and only need to verify the supplied size, a readable label might suffice. If the listing uses an unfamiliar chart and fit is the deciding factor, a measurement gathered with a clear method could be worth requesting.
Establish a reference from a shoe that fits

Choose a shoe you wear comfortably for the same activity. If it has a removable insert that comes out without damage, take it out and note its shape. Place it on a flat surface and measure the straight distance from the rear edge at the heel to the longest point of the toe. Keep the ordinary shape of the insert and avoid pulling it longer. If the insert is contoured, note how you positioned it. Take a photograph showing the ruler and the entire insert, so that later you can ask for a comparable view.

Record the reference shoe's marked size and system, the measured length, which side you measured and the unit. If the reference insert has a different outline or thickness from the new shoe, write that down too. A narrow pointed toe and a broad rounded toe can create different usable space despite matching overall length. Measuring a foot is a separate exercise. If you decide to use a seller's foot-length chart, follow its specified method and compare your foot to that chart rather than silently converting an insole measurement into a body measurement.
Keep the request tied to the purchased pair

Open the USFans order or warehouse record and confirm the exact seller option, colour and size. Two sizes of the same model can be impossible to distinguish from a front photograph. A picture from a similar pair on a spreadsheet is useful for deciding what to ask but does not identify what arrived for your order. Note the warehouse reference along with the seller item ID. Include the current order reference in an inquiry so the agent knows which physical pair requires attention.

USFans's beginner guide describes inspection at warehouse receipt and access to stored items. Use the current order channel to check whether a particular measurement or additional photograph is available. Establish any fee before requesting the service. Ask the handler to remove an insert only if it is designed to come out easily and the requested handling is permitted. Glued or fixed components should stay in place. In that situation, choose an alternative source of evidence, such as a readable size label or a clearly described internal measurement, and record what method was actually used.
Give the photographer an instruction with visible endpoints

A useful request might say, “For the blue pair in this warehouse entry, please show the marked size and, if the insert is readily removable, photograph one insert beside a metric ruler. Show the heel edge, longest toe point, zero mark and final reading together.” This separates identification from measurement. If the handler can supply two pictures, use one overview for the whole arrangement and a closer image only when needed to read small markings. A close-up alone can make a wrong endpoint appear convincing.

Check the returned picture before interpreting it. Is the ruler straight and in the same plane as the insert? Is the zero at the edge or beyond it? Is the final reading in centimetres or inches? A ruler positioned at an angle or photographed from the side can create an apparent difference. Some rulers begin before their printed zero. If the heel aligns with one centimetre and the toe with twenty-eight centimetres, the observed interval is twenty-seven centimetres. That example illustrates why the two endpoints matter more than the final numeral.
Compare equivalent measurements and note the uncertainty

Put the two photographs side by side. Imagine your reference insert measures 27.2 cm and the new photographed insert appears to measure 27.4 cm using a comparable method. The visible difference is about 2 mm. A slightly curved insert, a different camera angle or an imprecise ruler position can account for small differences. Avoid turning a rough photo comparison into an exact fit guarantee. By contrast, a clear multi-centimetre difference with matching methods would justify checking the size label and asking whether the photographed pair is the intended option.

If one photo shows an outsole and the other a removed insert, suspend the comparison. Explain which view you need and why. If both show inserts but one has a high heel cup that will not lie flat, ask how it was positioned and reproduce the same method on your reference shoe if possible. A result that remains uncertain is still informative: you know what the available evidence cannot establish. It is safer to make a conscious choice on limited evidence than to misread an incompatible number as reassurance.
Use the result in a purchasing decision

When the marked size, seller chart and comparable measurement all point in the same direction, note that agreement with the order. If the marked size matches but the insert differs substantially, inspect whether the chart referred to foot length, whether the seller changed model construction or whether there is a reference error. If the size label is visibly wrong, send the paid selection and the label photo together. Describe the discrepancy without speculating about why it occurred. Request the options available for the current order while the pair is still accessible for inspection.

Keep the packaging and any supplied inserts together until the question is settled. If you consider returning or exchanging the pair, check the applicable seller and agent conditions before altering or discarding anything. If you proceed with shipping despite an unresolved width or shape question, record that as part of the decision. Later, when you try the pair on, note which measurement predicted the fit and which limitation mattered. That small piece of first-hand evidence can make the next comparison more informative than another list of size conversions copied from an unrelated listing.
Preserve the date and model code as well. A later version of a similarly named shoe may use a different last, insert or upper construction, and its chart deserves a fresh check.

Record whether you wore a separate insert or a particularly thick sock during the comparison. A buyer replacing the supplied insert with their own will make a different fit decision from someone evaluating the shoe exactly as supplied.
Matching several USFans warehouse orders to one outbound parcel

When five shopping-cart lines turn into three warehouse records and one international parcel, a count of references stops being a count of physical items. Build the relationship from the items outward so you can tell what was packed, what is still waiting and what any later tracking update refers to.
Start with a list of physical pieces

Read each paid selection and write down what the seller agreed to supply. Include size, colour, quantity and whether the selected unit contains several pieces. Two pairs of socks and one two-piece outfit may be three order units but six individual pieces if you count each sock and each garment separately. Choose the counting unit that helps you check delivery and write it beside the number. “Two retail pairs” is clearer than “two” when reconciling small items. Keep the product link for identification but use the paid option as the primary description of the actual order.

Give each intended unit or group a short label that stays stable throughout the process. For instance, label a navy jacket J1 and the two matching trousers T1 and T2. Use warehouse and parcel identifiers alongside these labels as they become available. Do not replace the labels with successive tracking numbers. Identifiers from different stages often have different scopes: one buyer order can cover several seller deliveries, and one outbound parcel can cover several buyer orders. A stable per-item reference lets you connect all these records without assuming they share the same numbering system.
Connect seller delivery to warehouse intake

For each seller shipment, record the seller name, domestic carrier and tracking number if given. Identify the associated paid items and mark whether the seller claims the shipment is complete or split. A carrier delivery scan confirms a transport event for that package. The USFans warehouse entry is a separate event linking received goods to your account. A package can reach the facility before all its items appear in the warehouse view. If a shipment appears missing, begin with the last stage you can verify instead of assuming the international parcel is delayed.

Use warehouse photographs and option labels to match received entries to your intended-piece list. A photograph of a plain black T-shirt may not distinguish two sizes. Check the visible label or ask which entry corresponds to which size. If a single warehouse record contains multiple pieces, annotate the relationship beside that record. If one outfit arrives in two shipments, list both warehouse references beside the outfit label. This simple many-to-many mapping reduces the temptation to tick an entire order as complete as soon as its first component appears.
Decide which entries are ready for this parcel

Before submitting anything, review the state of each intended piece. Separate items you have accepted from items awaiting clarification, a further photo, a return or an exchange. Read any storage deadline against the individual warehouse entry. Waiting briefly for one delivery might be sensible, while waiting for every future order can create a storage or after-sales problem for earlier arrivals. USFans describes stored items under Warehouse and outgoing shipments as parcels. Use the live status in the appropriate part of your account rather than inferring readiness from the seller's marketplace page.

Think about the physical dependencies between entries. If a removable hood was supplied separately from a jacket, both pieces need to travel if the outfit is to be used as intended. Conversely, a replacement garment and the original garment awaiting return should not both enter the same outbound parcel simply because they look similar. Mark the exact item to go and the action still pending on the other. Review route eligibility and packing needs for all selected contents, especially where one item could affect the route choice or protection needed for the rest.
Create a parcel manifest you can read later

Write a short packing manifest before submitting the parcel. Include each warehouse reference, item description and physical quantity. Note whether retail packaging is to remain, any protection you requested and any accessory expected inside a larger item. Save a copy before changing the selection. When the outbound parcel reference is issued, add it to the manifest. Keep the route, destination and date next to that reference. A written content list makes a future support message much easier to interpret than a series of screenshots with no explanation of which stage they depict.

Consider an example with four wearable items. Warehouse entry A holds a jacket with its detachable hood. Entry B contains two shirts, size small and medium. Entry C is a cap that has yet to arrive. If you submit A and B today, the parcel covers three wearable items plus the hood that belongs to the jacket. C stays outside this shipment. Record the cap as pending rather than lost. If the two shirts are folded together inside the same protective bag, note that packaging arrangement so you know what to look for when the parcel is opened.
Reconcile parcel measurements and tracking

The manifest identifies what you intend to ship. The parcel measurements describe the packed result. Keep item-level weights, package dimensions and outbound billing information distinct. Adding individual estimates will not necessarily reproduce the measured weight of the final box because packing materials, removed packaging or later adjustments can change it. If the final figure seems surprising, first compare the actual selected contents with your own manifest. An extra warehouse entry or a retained retail box may explain an apparent difference without any carrier error.

Track the outbound shipment using the carrier and reference shown for that parcel. A domestic seller number may already show delivered, even while the international parcel is only being prepared. If a carrier hands the parcel to a local delivery partner, record the second number against the same manifest when the tracking information identifies it. A new tracking reference does not automatically mean a second physical parcel exists. Look for confirmation of a split or additional package before creating an extra entry in your inventory or assuming something was left behind.
Check arrival without reconstructing the order from memory

When the parcel arrives, keep the outer packaging and label while checking the contents against your list. Locate each item, its option and any small accessories that might be tucked inside retail packaging. If a piece appears absent, compare the warehouse photo and packing instruction before discarding wrapping. Record whether the outer parcel arrived damaged, whether interior packing was disturbed and what remains present. A photograph showing the whole contents beside the packaging is useful context for closer images of a missing set component or damaged item.

If a discrepancy remains, contact the relevant support channel with the outbound parcel reference, the affected warehouse reference and the missing or incorrect piece. Explain what had been confirmed before dispatch and what you observed at delivery. Keep unrelated pending seller shipments separate from the case. Once everything is reconciled, mark each physical item received, refunded, replaced or still pending. The final manifest then tells a reliable story from original purchase to arrival, even when the number of cart lines, warehouse entries and carrier references never matched.

For a shared purchase, also identify who expects each item without putting unnecessary personal details in a public spreadsheet. A private initial or order label is enough. Record how any shared shipping amount was apportioned separately from the carrier charge itself. This prevents an internal budget calculation from being mistaken later for an actual cost billed on a specific warehouse entry.
Checking translated colour options before a USFans purchase

The option menu says grey, the picture looks green and the seller's colour code ends in G2. Which of these describes the item you will actually receive? Work from the seller's option identity, then use photographs to answer the remaining questions about appearance.
Save the identity of the option first

Start at the live marketplace listing linked from the USFans page. Write down the shop, item identifier, selected size and original colour wording. Include any suffix, model code or number printed beside the colour. Sellers sometimes use colour selectors to distinguish construction, material, size ranges or packages as well as hue. Two options translated to “black” can represent different linings or versions. Keep the original wording and the translated description beside each other so that a later change in translation does not erase the distinction you used to choose.

Now choose a neighbouring swatch and watch what happens. Does the selected text change? Does the main photograph change? Does moving back to the desired option restore both the previous picture and the price? This checks that the selected state is tied to the intended option rather than simply viewing the next image in a gallery. Save a screenshot that shows the selected label together with the item, size and visible identifying details. A crop containing only a square of colour gives someone reviewing an order little basis for choosing the correct version.
Read labels as seller vocabulary

Colour words rarely map neatly from one language to another. A seller may use a marketing name, a factory code and an everyday colour description together. A translated “rice white” and “white” might indicate a warmer cream and a brighter white, or the text may refer to two entirely different versions. Treat this as a question about the seller's catalogue. Search for another labelled image or swatch within that listing, and compare how the seller uses the same words across adjacent options. Avoid imposing your preferred interpretation of a marketing name on the actual offer.

Suppose a listing includes navy A and navy B. One promotional picture shows contrast stitching and another shows matching stitching. The wearable distinction you care about might be stitching, even though the selector calls both options navy. Ask “Which navy option has the contrast stitching shown beside the zip?” instead of “Which blue is darker?” A concrete feature gives the seller a way to identify the option even under different lighting. If no physical feature separates the two choices in the pictures, ask for a labelled side-by-side view or code confirmation where available before paying.
Use photographs with a realistic understanding of colour

Compare more than one image of the same option. Check whether the seller edited some pictures heavily or photographed the garment against strongly coloured backgrounds. Daylight, warm indoor light and camera processing can change the appearance of a neutral item in opposite directions. Your display settings add another variable. Identify differences that remain visible across views: a contrasting cuff, two-tone panel, differently coloured zip or distinct fabric weave. These can be more reliable identifiers than the apparent saturation of one image.

If matching another garment matters, work with evidence in the same frame where possible. A pair of trousers photographed under warm warehouse lights and a jacket photographed outdoors are poor material for an exact shade comparison. A request for both pieces together in one picture may resolve whether they visibly coordinate, provided both are available and belong to the correct orders. Even then, fabric texture and direction can affect how the same dye looks on camera. Decide in advance whether you need exact shade matching or simply two pieces that look acceptable together.
Keep the order note unambiguous

USFans describes choosing colour, size and quantity before submitting an order. After selecting the desired combination, inspect the cart and final summary. A saved product link may reopen on the seller's default option, so recheck just before paying. In the order note, record the seller's original option text, the option code and a short description of the distinguishing feature. If you are ordering multiple colours, state the desired quantity for each on separate lines. A note saying “one of each” becomes unclear as soon as a seller adds, removes or reorders swatches.

For a two-colour purchase, an illustrative note could read “one G2 grey-green medium with dark zip, and one C1 cream medium with cream zip.” Ask before accepting a substitution if the intended colour is unavailable. Someone filling the order may read two similar translations and treat a nearby option as interchangeable, while the buyer needs a matching piece for an existing outfit. Giving both the code and feature reduces this risk without claiming a colour standard that the seller never promised. Save the confirmation beside the selected-state screenshot.
Determine what the warehouse can establish

Once the order arrives, open the photographs associated with that order or warehouse entry. Compare the option label or packaging code with the confirmation first. Then inspect the relevant visible feature and overall appearance. If the code and construction match but the hue looks unexpected, seek another view before concluding that the physical item is wrong. If the label clearly names a different option, include that label and the paid selection in an order inquiry. The evidence for a different code is stronger than two pictures that merely look different on your screen.

Ask a specific question if the first photo cannot resolve an important distinction. “Please show the option label and both sides of the sleeve stripe on warehouse item [reference]” identifies actionable evidence. “Please prove the colour is right” leaves the photographer guessing at lighting, angle and the buyer's expectation. Check availability and terms of any additional service in the live order. If the garment is sealed and opening it might matter to a return, ask before authorizing opening. Keep the deadline and conditions for any after-sales decision separate from the storage period for that item.
Decide what uncertainty you can accept

Before approving international shipment, put the evidence into three groups: what you ordered, what the received item's label says, and how the item looks in the available lighting. If all three point to the intended option, record the result. If the first and second disagree, ask the agent to check fulfilment. If the label matches but the appearance remains uncertain, decide whether a new view would change your choice. Include the original order reference in any request so that a photograph of another buyer's similar piece does not enter the comparison unnoticed.

For a future purchase, preserve the option name and code rather than renaming the record with a broad translation. Add the date, seller reference and a note about how the colour looked in person once the garment arrives. A later listing from the same shop can still use different cloth, photography or option names, so treat that note as a useful starting point. The most reliable outcome is a trail connecting your selected option, the seller's vocabulary and the item actually received, with any uncertainty about shade honestly documented along the way.
That distinction is particularly useful on repeat orders, where a remembered English nickname may persist long after the seller has changed the underlying option or photograph.

If you give the item to someone else, retain that same distinction in your description. A precise seller code can help another buyer find a close candidate, while an observation such as “looked warmer beside my cream shirt in daylight” honestly describes a personal comparison.
One seller, two deliveries: tracing a split shipment to the USFans warehouse

A seller can send two packages for one purchase, while the first carrier scan makes the whole order look delivered. To find out what remains outstanding, connect each expected piece to a specific domestic shipment and each shipment to a warehouse entry.
Define the delivery you are trying to trace

First distinguish the delivery from the Chinese seller to the warehouse from the later international parcel. The seller's tracking number normally describes a domestic leg. A delivery scan on that number can therefore mean delivery to the receiving facility in China. It does not establish that the buyer's international parcel has been submitted or delivered. USFans's beginner guide separates seller purchasing, warehouse inspection and the later parcel stage. Check the part of your account corresponding to the stage you are investigating before interpreting a tracking status.

Write down what the seller was expected to supply under the paid selections. Include the quantity, option and any set components. If three shirts in different sizes and one belt were purchased, enter the four physical items separately. Group them under the agent order number without assuming they all shared one seller package. Add the original product links or item identifiers beside the lines. If a seller or agent sends a tracking number later, there will then be a specific inventory for that number to explain rather than an undocumented expectation that the order should somehow be complete.
Identify evidence of an actual split

Look for an explicit seller message naming separate parcels, multiple domestic tracking numbers or delivery information that connects particular order lines to different shipments. Two status updates on a single number can simply be two scans of the same parcel. Two different numbers can also describe a handoff or corrected label, so ask which physical packages they represent when the seller's explanation is unclear. Save the original carrier name, number and dates instead of copying only the current status into your notes. A status can change; the identifying reference lets you revisit its history.

Suppose the seller says a jacket shipped today and the matching trousers will follow tomorrow. This is evidence of an intended split but does not yet identify the second parcel. Record the jacket's tracking reference if supplied and mark the trousers as awaiting domestic tracking. Ask for their reference after dispatch. If the seller supplies one number for both pieces, ask whether they were packed together. The question concerns the number of physical packages and the contents attributed to each one. A seller order number reused in two messages does not answer it.
Match each package to warehouse intake

Open the USFans warehouse records and inspect what has actually been identified. A single package may produce a record containing several units, while two seller packages can appear as separate entries. Read the item description and look at identifying labels in the photographs. A pile of similar folded garments can hide which sizes were received. Mark only the pieces you can match and identify what remains unclear. If a package was expected to include a small accessory inside a jacket pocket, note that location before assuming the item is absent from the overview photo.

Maintain a short timeline. Record seller dispatch, carrier delivery scan, warehouse intake and the time the photographs became available as separate events. When one carrier package has been delivered and the warehouse has identified the correct garment, close that part of the inquiry. When another shows only label creation or pickup, continue following that specific number. If delivery was reported but warehouse intake remains unexplained, verify destination, recipient details permitted for the inquiry and carrier reference with the seller or agent. A chronological account makes the uncertain stage clear without inventing a responsibility for the problem.
Use a worked example to locate the missing step

Imagine an order with shirts in small and medium plus a detachable belt. The seller confirms parcel A contains both shirts and parcel B contains the belt. Parcel A reaches the warehouse and the available photographs show two shirts, but only the small label is visible. Parcel B is still moving. Record the two received shirt units while flagging the medium label for verification. Record the belt as in transit. There are two unresolved questions, and they require different actions: a label check at the warehouse and a tracking check for the separate domestic shipment.

Now suppose the seller later says the belt was actually placed inside parcel A. Preserve the original statement and record the correction with its date. Ask the warehouse to check the relevant packaging or pocket before it is discarded. Ask whether parcel B is still in transit and what it contains if the belt travelled in A. Avoid silently editing the expected contents of both packages, because that can make the original discrepancy impossible to explain. A correction linked to its source is more useful than an apparently tidy record that no longer shows why anyone searched for the wrong package.
Communicate without opening overlapping inquiries

Send one message that identifies the paid order and the exact unresolved line. Include the domestic carrier and tracking number, the seller's description of its contents and the last event you can verify. If a warehouse reference already exists, supply that as well. For instance: “Parcel A was received under warehouse entry W. The two shirts are visible; could you check the medium label? The seller says the belt travelled separately under B, which still shows domestic transit.” A recipient can route the two questions correctly without having to reconstruct the order from a series of screenshots.

If a seller proposes a resend, establish which original pieces it will replace and whether the original shipment could still arrive. Ask for the replacement tracking reference once dispatched. Keep it beside the original number and mark it specifically as a resend. Two independently arriving units could be a replacement and its delayed original rather than two items the buyer intended to export. Check with the agent about handling a duplicate before combining either one with an international parcel. Preserve any packaging the seller may request for a return while the case remains unsettled.
Decide when to submit the international parcel

Once the warehouse has identified the expected entries, check each item that needs a quality or option decision. The arrival of the last domestic package does not resolve an earlier question about size or damage. If you prefer to ship accepted pieces before a missing item arrives, compare current packing and freight options for a split outbound shipment. The seller's domestic split and the buyer's international parcel choice are independent. Two seller packages can ultimately travel together internationally if the agent and chosen route permit it.

Finish by marking the disposition of every originally expected unit: received and selected for shipping, received but waiting, returned, refunded, or still in transit. If the seller refunded a missing component, remove it from the expected international contents without describing it as received. Add the outbound parcel reference only to entries actually submitted. This closes the domestic tracking question and creates a clean record for the next stage. Should the final international package appear short, you can then identify precisely whether the missing line ever reached the warehouse and whether it was among the items chosen for dispatch.

The same separation helps with a shared order. Someone waiting for the belt can see its own last verified event without interpreting the received shirts as proof that every purchase has arrived or expecting the seller's tracking number to follow the final international delivery.
